title: Message Structure and Serialization
description: Learn how to design well-structured messages with headers, bodies, and appropriate serialization formats for inter-service communication.

data.text: A message is more than just a payload. It includes metadata (headers), a body (the actual data), and often a content-type declaration. Designing your message structure carefully ensures interoperability, observability, and resilience across distributed systems. Poorly structured messages become a hidden coupling point between services.

Most message brokers model a message with three main parts: headers for metadata, a body for the payload, and attributes like message ID, timestamp, and correlation ID. Headers carry routing hints, tracing identifiers, and custom properties without requiring the consumer to deserialize the body first.

terms.definition: Key-value metadata pairs on a message. Used for routing, tracing, priority, and content-type declarations.
The serialized payload of the message. Can be JSON, binary, or text depending on the format.
An identifier that links related messages, typically used to trace a request across multiple services.
A header declaring the serialization format (e.g., application/json, application/x-protobuf) so consumers know how to deserialize the body.

data.text: JSON is the most common message format because it is human-readable, language-agnostic, and supported everywhere. However, JSON lacks a formal schema, so schema evolution is handled by convention rather than enforcement. Include a version field in the body to support backward-compatible changes.

data.title: Well-Structured JSON Message in C#
data.content: Always include headers for cross-cutting concerns and a typed body for the domain data.

data.text: Protocol Buffers (protobuf) is a binary serialization format developed by Google. It is significantly smaller and faster than JSON, and it enforces a schema through .proto files. Use protobuf when message volume is high, latency is critical, or you need strict schema contracts between services.

data.title: Schema Evolution with Protobuf
data.text: Protobuf supports backward and forward compatibility. Never remove or reuse field numbers. Add new fields as optional to maintain compatibility with older consumers.

data.title: Message Body Best Practices
items: Keep the body self-contained; do not require consumers to call external APIs for context
Include an event type or action field (e.g., 'order.created') so consumers can route internally
Add a version number to handle schema evolution gracefully
Never include secrets, passwords, or raw connection strings in the body
Use UTC timestamps consistently; never mix local and UTC times
Prefer snake_case or camelCase consistently across all message contracts

data.title: Avoid Over-Loading Headers
data.text: Headers are not designed for large payloads. Keep headers under 1 KB. If you need to send large metadata, include it in the body or use a reference to an external store like S3 or Azure Blob Storage.

items.question: Should I use headers or the body for metadata?
items.answer: Use headers for metadata that routing or filtering systems need without deserializing the body. Use the body for domain-specific data.

items.question: Is protobuf worth the complexity?
items.answer: Protobuf pays off when you have high message volumes, strict latency requirements, or need formal schema contracts. For simple microservice communication, JSON with OpenAPI is often sufficient.

items.question: How do I handle multiple schema versions?
items.answer: Use a version field in the body and support both old and new fields. Consumers should ignore unknown fields. Never remove fields; only add new optional ones.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Messages have headers, a body, and broker metadata
Headers are for routing and tracing; the body carries domain data
JSON is flexible and readable; protobuf is compact and schema-driven
Always version your message schemas for safe evolution
data.takeaway: Good message design reduces coupling and makes distributed systems easier to evolve and debug.

data.title: Design a PaymentProcessed Event
data.description: Design a message schema for a PaymentProcessed event that will be consumed by three services: an email service, an analytics service, and an order service. Include headers, a versioned body, and decide on a serialization format.
steps: Define the headers needed for routing and tracing
Design the body fields (paymentId, orderId, amount, status, timestamp)
Choose a serialization format and justify your choice
Consider how you will handle a future 'refundId' field without breaking consumers
data.expectedOutcome: You have a complete message contract with headers and body that can evolve over time.
